<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="28" type="chapter">
                  <ns0:head>CHAP. XXVIII.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 AND Isaac called Jacob, and blessed him <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Confirm'd his former blessing, being now thoroughly sen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sible both of Gods purpose, and of his own Duty, wishing him also a prosperous and successful journey; as the word is used, <ns0:hi>Ios.</ns0:hi> 22. 7.</ns0:note>, and charged him; and said unto him, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 24. 3.</ns0:note> Thou shalt not take a wife of the daughters of Canaan.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Hos. 12. 12.</ns0:note> Arise, go to Padan-aram, to the house of Bethuel <ns0:note n="‖" place="bottom">See <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 22. 22, 23. and 25. 20.</ns0:note>, thy mothers father, and take thee a wife from thence of the daughters of <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 24. 29.</ns0:note> Laban thy mothers brother.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 And God Almighty bless thee, and make thee fruitful, and multiply thee, that thou mayest be <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> an assem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bly of people.</ns0:note> a multitude of people:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 And give thee <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 12. 2.</ns0:note> the Blessing of Abraham, to thee, and to thy seed with thee, that thou mayest inherit the Land <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> of thy so<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />journing.</ns0:note> wherein thou art a stranger, which God gave unto Abraham.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 And Isaac sent away Jacob, and he went to Padan-aram, unto Laban, son of Bethuel the Sy<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rian <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Obj.</ns0:hi> He was no <ns0:hi>Syrian</ns0:hi> but a <ns0:hi>Mesopotamian.</ns0:hi> Ans. <ns0:hi>Syria</ns0:hi> is sometimes largely taken and so it comprehends <ns0:hi>Mesopotamia</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Chaldea,</ns0:hi> yea and <ns0:hi>Assyria,</ns0:hi> as appears from <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 36. 11. <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 2. 4.</ns0:note>, the brother of Rebekah, Jacobs and E<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />saus mother.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 When Esau saw that Isaac had blessed Jacob, and sent him away to Padan-aram, to take him a wife from thence, and that as he blessed him, he gave him a charge, saying, Thou shalt not take a wife of the daughters of Canaan.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 And that Jacob obeyed his Father, and his mother, and was gone to Padan-aram:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 And Esau seeing that the daughters of Ca<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />naan <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>were evil in the eyes,</ns0:hi> &c.</ns0:note> pleased not Isaac his Father:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 Then went Esau unto Ishmael <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Either to his Person; or, rather to his Family called <ns0:hi>Ishma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />el</ns0:hi> by their Fathers name, as <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> is sometimes put for <ns0:hi>Da<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vids</ns0:hi> posterity: for <ns0:hi>Ishmael</ns0:hi> seems to have been dead before this, from <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 25. 17. though that may possibly be a Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lepsis, and then this may be <ns0:hi>Ishmael</ns0:hi> himself.</ns0:note>, and took unto the wives which he had, Mahalath <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Called also <ns0:hi>Bashemath, Gen.</ns0:hi> 36. 3. He thought by this means to ingratiate him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self with his Father, and so to get another and a better bles<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sing: but he takes no care to reconcile himself to God, nor observes his hand in the business. Besides he mends one fault by committing another and taking a third wife when he had one too many before, and her too he unwisely fetcheth out of that stock which was begotten to bondage and was ut<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />terly uncapable of the inheritance.</ns0:note>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> the daughter of Ishmael Abrahams son, the sister of Nebajoth <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Ishmaels</ns0:hi> eldest son, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 25. 13. who alone is here mentioned, either in the name of all the rest, whose Sister she is by consequence supposed to be; or because peradventure she and <ns0:hi>Nebajoth</ns0:hi> were <ns0:hi>Ishmaels</ns0:hi> chil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dren by the same Mother, and the rest by another.</ns0:note>, to be his wife.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 And Jacob went <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">It is not strange that <ns0:hi>Iacob</ns0:hi> went alone, as it appears that he did from <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 32. 10. when his Grandfathers servant was at<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tended with a great retinue, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 24. because attendance was then necessary to procure him Reputation and to obtain the consent of the Virgin and her Parents to so long a journey, but here as it was unnecessary, so it would have been troublesome and prejudicial, exposing him both to the envy and snares of his brother <ns0:hi>Esau,</ns0:hi> which by this private departure he did a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />void. Besides God in his wise Providence did so order this and some other matters of the like nature, for the greater illu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stration of his care and kindness towards his Children. Add to this the great simplicity, humility, and innocency of those times if compared with ours, which made many things then usual which now would be ridiculous.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Hos. 12. 12.</ns0:note> out from Beer-sheba, and went toward <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">called Acts 7. 2. <ns0:hi>Charran.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> Haran.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 And he lighted upon a certain place, and tarried there all night, because the sun was set: and he took of the stones of that place, and put <ns0:hi>them for</ns0:hi> his pillows, and lay down in that place to sleep.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 And he dreamed, and behold, a ladder set upon the earth, and the top of it reached to hea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven: and behold, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Heb. 1. 14.</ns0:note> the Angels of God ascending and descending on it <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">This Ladder may be considered, either 1. Literally, and so it represented to <ns0:hi>Iacob</ns0:hi> the Providence of God, who though he dwell in heaven extends his care and government to the earth, and particularly makes use of the Angels as ministring Spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rits for the good of his People. And these Angels do not appear idle, or standing still, but always in motion, either ascending to God to receive his commands, or descending to Earth for the Execution of them. Which was a most season<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />able Vision for <ns0:hi>Iacob</ns0:hi> in his sad and sorrowful condition, that he might see, that though he was forsaken and persecuted by men, and forced to flee away secretly for fear of his life, yet he neither was nor should be neglected or forsaken by God in this whole Journey. Or 2. Mystically, and so it represents Christ, by whom Heaven and Earth are united, who is called <ns0:hi>the way</ns0:hi> to Heaven, which this Ladder was, who, as the head of Angels, is perpetually sending them forth either to God or from God to Minister to the Heirs of Salvation. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 1. 14. And this explication or accommodation of this Vision is war<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ranted by our Saviour himself, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 1. 51.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 35. 1. and 48. 3.</ns0:note> And behold, the LORD stood above it, and said, I <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> the LORD God of Abraham thy father, and the God of Isaac: the land, whereon thou liest, to thee will I give it, and to thy seed.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 And thy seed shall be as the dust of the earth, and thou shalt <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> break forth.</ns0:note> spread abroad <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Deut. 12. 20.</ns0:note> to the west, and to the east, and to the north, and to the south: and in thee, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 12. 3. and 18. 18. and 22. 18. & 26. 4.</ns0:note> in thy seed, shall all the Families <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>(i. e.)</ns0:hi> The Nations, as that word is used.</ns0:note> of the earth be blessed.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 And behold, I am with thee, and will keep thee in all <ns0:hi>places</ns0:hi> whither thou goest, and will bring thee again into this land: for I will not leave thee untill I have done that which I have spoken to thee of <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Nor ever after: for so the word <ns0:hi>until</ns0:hi> is frequently used, as 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 6. 23. <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 1. 25. not so as to exclude the time fol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lowing, but so as to include all the foregoing time, wherein the thing spoken of might be most suspected or feared, as here the worst and most dangerous state in which <ns0:hi>Iacob</ns0:hi> was or was like to be was this time of his Banishment from his Country and Kindred, against which he is therefore particularly armed and comforted in these words.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 And Jacob awaked out of his sleep, and he said: Surely the LORD is in this place <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">By his special and gracious presence and the manifestation of his Mind and Will to me.</ns0:note>, and I knew it not <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">I little expected to meet with such a Revelation out of my Fathers House, much less in this desart and doleful state and place, when I thought my self re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />jected by God as well as abandoned by men.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 And he was afraid, and said, How dreadful <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>venerable,</ns0:hi> both for the Majesty of the Person present, and for the glorious manner of his discovery of himself.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> this place? this is none other, but the house of God <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">The Habitation of God and of his Holy Angels.</ns0:note>, and this <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the gate of heaven.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 And Jacob rose up early in the morning, and took the stone that he had put for his pillows, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 31. 45. and 35. 14.</ns0:note> set it up for a pillar <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">As a Monument of Gods great kindness and gracious mani<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />festation of himself to him; which might bring this Mercy to his remembrance in his return, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 31. 13. This was an anti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ent practise among the Patriarchs, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 35. 14. but afterwards upon the growing abuse of it among the Heathens, it was for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bidden by God, <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 26. 1. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 7. 5. and 12. 3.</ns0:note>, and poured oil <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Which he brought with him either for Food or Medicine or for the anointing of himself, as need required.</ns0:note> upon the top of it <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">As a token of his consecration thereof to this use to be a memorial of Gods favour to him. Oil was used in Sacrifices, and in the consecration of Persons and Places, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 30. 25, 26. and 40. 9.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:29" />19 And he called the name of <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Judg. 1. 23, 20. Hos. 4. 15.</ns0:note> that place <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">That is, <ns0:hi>the house of God.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> Beth-el: but the name of that City <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Either of that City which was nearest to the Field in which <ns0:hi>Iacob</ns0:hi> lay: or of that City which afterwards was built in or near to this place, and was known by the name of <ns0:hi>Bethel.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> was cal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led Luz, at the first.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 And Jacob vowed a vow <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>(i. e.)</ns0:hi> Bound himself by a solemn promise or obligation. Compare <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 14. 22. <ns0:hi>Eccles.</ns0:hi> 5. 4.</ns0:note>, saying, If God will be with me <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">He speaks not thus as if he doubted of the truth of Gods Promises, or would like a mercenary Person make a bargain with God, but rather suppos<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth that God will do this for him, as he had in effect promised <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 15. and thereupon obligeth himself to a grateful return to God for this Mercy, <ns0:hi>If God will be with me,</ns0:hi> &c. as he hath just now assured me he will: or <ns0:hi>seeing God will be with me,</ns0:hi> &c. for the Hebrew <ns0:hi>im</ns0:hi> doth not alwayes imply a doubt, but rather a sup<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />position, and is oft rendered <ns0:hi>seeing that,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 20. 25. <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 36. 4. 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 15. 17. <ns0:hi>Amos</ns0:hi> 7. 2. And so the Greek particle answering to the Hebrew <ns0:hi>im</ns0:hi> is used <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 6. 22. <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 11. 34.</ns0:note>, and will keep me in this way that I go, and will give me <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Tim. 6. 8.</ns0:note> bread <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Food convenient,</ns0:hi> as it is called <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 30. 8. which is oft signify<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed by the name of <ns0:hi>Bread,</ns0:hi> See <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 3. 19.</ns0:note> to eat, and raiment to put on,</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 So that I come again to my fathers house in peace: then shall the LORD be my God <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">I will publickly own him for my God and the Saviour of men, and will establish his solemn Worship, as it follows.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 And this stone which I have set for a pil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lar, shall be Gods house <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>(i. e.)</ns0:hi> A place where I will offer prayers and Sacrifices to God: such places being commonly called Gods houses, and God is oft sand to dwell in them, in regard of his special presence there. See <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 20. 24. Compare <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 17. of this chapter and <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 35. 1, 3, 7.</ns0:note>: and of all that thou shalt give me, I will surely give the tenth unto thee <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">To be laid out in thy service and for sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />crifices and for the use and benefit of those who shall attend upon sacred things, as also for the relief of the poor and needy, whom God hath substituted in his room, and to whom part of the Tithes were to be given by a following Law, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 14. 28, 29.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
